The concept of the operator is super interesting. But unfortunately there's not a lot to explore and investigate here. We're constantly guided by other characters and told the very thing we need to find, one thing after the next. It's like the game never gets past the tutorial, and it never gets to the point where you get to do more advanced research. This simple game mechanic is not super satisfying. It feels more like a short story turned into a game than a real detective game. It's on a very different level compared to other detective games such as Return of the Obra Dinn, The Roottrees are Dead or The Case of the Golden Idol. It's also very short, I finished it in less than 4 hours and there's no replayability. Also be very careful with the saves, there are save points and you'll lose progress if you don't quit at exactly the right times. On the plus side, the interface is quite well done and the voices are nice (though I'm not sure why it makes my computer boiling hot when the graphics are so simple). I liked the bomb defusing part the most, and it's a shame we can't replay that part again.

A complete disappointment.

1. The gameplay is primitive and boring. Games like Cyber Manhunt or Orwell do this concept much better, in my opinion—they’re more engaging and last longer. The cutscenes drag on, and while you can see why they're there for certain moments... those moments are painfully obvious within the first hour of playing and after that, they seem redundant.
2. The story is shallow and uninteresting. The main twist is something you figure out in the first hour—[spoiler]namely, that your protagonist is Sasha Cole (thanks to the opening scene, the emphasis on Mia COLE, and the fact that your character starts hallucinating when the agent recalls her love for singing). Once you realize that, it’s immediately clear that your friend is the mole, while the "obviously" unfriendly boss is actually a good guy.[/spoiler] This one dumb decision ruins the rest of the game—there’s no wow factor, no payoff.
3. The lore? There isn’t any. Nothing is properly revealed or explained. They just threw in a bunch of medical and chemical terms and called it a day. [spoiler]Who is the Ghost? Why can he effortlessly kill trained agents? What’s the deal with the Organization? The game explains nothing—guess we’ll have to wait for a sequel instead of getting a proper, finished story.[/spoiler]
4. The ending... It left me completely deflated. [spoiler]I hate "everybody dies" endings more than anything, especially when the game tries to pretend it’s being "nonlinear."[/spoiler]
5. It’s very short. Less than three hours to finish.

I absolutely loved The Operator. From the moment I stepped into Evan Tanner’s shoes, booting up that simulated desktop and diving into the role of a rookie operator at the Federal Department of Intelligence, I was hooked. The game didn’t just pull me into its world—it immersed me in a labyrinth of conspiracies, moral dilemmas, and surveillance, all wrapped in a retro ‘90s aesthetic with tech that felt eerily futuristic. It was nostalgic, yes, but also unsettling in the best way.

The gameplay was simple on the surface, but each task—analyzing grainy footage, cross-referencing databases, solving puzzles—made me feel like a true digital detective. It reminded me of Her Story, but stood firmly on its own legs with a tighter narrative and a mystery that grew darker and more complex with every click. The writing was spot-on, and the voice acting had a realism that drew me even deeper into the cases.

Honestly, my biggest gripe was that it ended too soon. I finished it in just a few hours, and while every minute was satisfying, I found myself wishing for more—more time in that richly constructed world, more twists, more layers. The cliffhanger at the end didn’t just tease a continuation; it practically begged for one. I’m really hoping Bureau 81 brings us a sequel that picks up right where the story left off.

Short as it was, The Operator delivered one of the most engaging and rewarding detective experiences I’ve played in ages. It made me pay attention, think critically, and trust my instincts. And I’d jump at the chance to return to that world the moment a sequel drops.

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 98:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆☆ (8/10)

[i] The Operator [/i] casts you not as a hero in the field, but as the analyst—the voice behind the computer—supporting agents from the shadows. It’s a fascinating setup and a fresh twist on crime-solving games, and usually almost always lives up to its potential!

🖥[b] Pros: [/b]
[list]
[*] Authentic "operator" fantasy. You monitor missions from your desk, field phone calls, look through mysterious documents, and scrub through CCTV footage. 

[*] Diverse tools. The game gives you a chem scanner, facial recognition database, image enhancement tech, and document search systems. For example, in one mission, you identify a suspect by cross-referencing a blurry security camera with an equally blurry security footage of his car and license plate. That kind of detective work feels cool. You feel smart when it works.

[*] Great use of puzzles under pressure. A standout moment has you guiding a field agent through bomb defusal. You have to analyze chemicals, check your reference files, and read out step-by-step instructions—all while the timer ticks down. These time-sensitive missions are where the game shines.

[*] Well-done audio design. The UI clicks, radio static, and phone calls all contribute to a grounded, late-'90s thriller vibe. The voice acting is low-key but sells the scenario well, especially during moments of stress or confusion.

[*] No filler. It’s tight and focused. No wandering, no padding. You’re thrown into the action quickly and missions move at a brisk pace.
[/list]

[b]🧾 Cons: [/b]
[list]
[*] Flat characters. The field agents and mysterious hacker HAL are more archetypes than flesh-and-blood. They push the story forward, but rarely surprise

[*] Choices don’t matter much. There are dialogue branches, but most are cosmetic. Whether you’re professional or snarky, or even whether you succeed or fail at certain puzzles, the game mostly funnels you into the same story beats.

[*] Abrupt ending. The game ends just as things get interesting. HAL’s storyline ramps up, then vanishes. You barely get to dig into the conspiracy or see the consequences of your actions. It feels like a miniseries that ends on episode three.
[/list]

Hello developers,

I just finished playing your game on the Switch, and I immediately bought the Steam version to add to my library. The game's atmosphere and narrative pacing really drew me in, and the background music was perfectly fitting. Because of this, I'm happy to leave a positive review, though it also left me with higher expectations.

 [spoiler]
The game is about four hours long, and playing it felt more like watching a movie. However, as a game, it offered too few choices for the player. During my play through, I tried to deliberately not answer the supervisor's calls or even pretended to be a 'good kid' to see if there was a way to betray HAL. But the game didn't give me any more options. I believe that in an interactive story game, player choices and their consequences are its true charm and what keeps players engaged.
The bomb disposal segment really stood out. I felt a strong sense of immersion and genuinely enjoyed being able to help someone. It's a shame that, probably due to the game's length, such a brilliant sequence only happened once.
The core puzzle was very cleverly designed, and its reveal was absolutely an adrenaline rush. I completely understand what you, as developers, wanted players to feel with that ending—the horror, the profound sense of melancholy, the sadness for the characters, and the lingering regret that a bigger enemy wasn't truly dealt with. However, even after experiencing all that, I still wished players could help the characters achieve a good ending. I truly love these characters.
Overall, this is a fantastic game! I really hope to play more from you in the future!
[/spoiler]

The Operator is a short but sweet game about assisting "FBI" agents while on cases, and uncovering a deeper conspiracy. 

The main gameplay is a mix of investigating cases using your FBI database and tools, and spotting contradicting parts of evidence. I enjoyed both the gameplay and the plot, and recommend this for anyone that thinks they would be interested.

Cons:

* The bomb defusal mission is just nonsensical. While it's obviously designed and written to be deliberately confusing to challenge the player, it is also ridiculous. The supervisor, Skinner, would be handling this, or at least offering assistance, not just casually leaving another agent's life up to a 3rd day employee who is reading the bomb defusal manual for the first time. Was having a good time in the game up until this mission. If you look at this achievement as well, only some ~50% of players have this achievement, and then you have to wonder, of those 50% how many had to look up a walk-through online in order to complete it? 
* Game was definitely somewhat dry at times where I felt a little bit bored. 
* I won't spoil any specifics but I will say the ending of the game is...not good, in my opinion. 

Pros:

* UI is clean and easy to use. The applications work smoothly without any issues. 
* Gameplay is straight forward and easy to understand. 
* Solid voice acting. 
* Storytelling is pretty engaging. 
* Game very stable, zero crashes or bugs / glitches. 
* No additional DRM beyond Steam.
* No Epic Online Services.

I got the game on sale and puzzle games aren't usually my thing but I wanted to give it a try as it sounded interesting and I like to support indie developers when I can, but this is a game that, despite some story aspects being well-done, the ending soured things for me as well as the bomb defusal mission to the point that I really would not recommend the game to others.

Okay, while I said I liked this game, [b]I think in terms of recommendation, this is more a "maybe" than an outright "yes."[/b] There are several things to consider before you purchase this one, and while I ultimately think you'll enjoy the experience either way, you may be slightly frustrated by at least one or two of these points. I know I was. 

(-) First, the game is short. It took me less than 4 hours to finish it, and that's with several long cut scenes. Speaking of those cut scenes... pay attention to them. I didn't, because some of them seemed pointless, and that led me to the only time I felt truly stuck in this game LOL.

(+) You play as an operator in the FDI, and the entire gameplay involves sitting in front of your computer, connecting dots, and solving puzzles. I absolutely loved it. It was fresh and interesting, and the feeling of things connecting and unraveling was really fun. I actually wish we had more of it—I would've gladly played more hours of more cases, slowly connecting them to this huge conspiracy. It made me hope that someone would make an entire mystery murder game (as opposed to a conspiracy) as "the guy in the chair," slowly unraveling everything and helping the "heroes" solve the mystery. 

(-/+) For a game that's sitting in front of your computer... the stakes are high and so is the tension. I actually got really anxious at parts, in a way that doesn't really happen with most games because, the way everything is set up, WE are Tenner. So I felt like there was a gun aimed at [i]me[/i] at times, LOL. For me, this was a point in favor of the game, but if you're looking for a more relaxed experience, this may not be it. 

(-/+) The ending. Personally? Not a fan. Oh, I loved the reveal. The minute [i]I[/i] started connecting the dots, my stomach dropped. 10/10 for that. But everything after that?... I will be playing the next game, if there is one, but overall, [spoiler]I am not really the kind of person to enjoy an "everybody died" ending. After all the brilliant puzzle solving, I wanted these characters to have a good ending. I have seen people talk about how this was actually a good ending - how Hal is still thwarting the organization 30 years later, and that's realistic and optimistic but damn. I got attached to [i]these[/i] characters. I wanted to see them happy, even if we fail to totally crush the bad guys in the end of the game. And I wanted to understand what the goal of the "bad guys" in this game is, and I don't. They're evil people, but... why are they doing what they're doing? No clue. Which is another thing I don't like. For me, a game needs to be able to stand on its own, even if it's part of a larger narrative. [/spoiler] Essentially, this felt like a game meant to [i]set up[/i] another game, and truthfully, I don't like that.

This is like the walking simulator of detective games. Don't go into this game expecting deduction gameplay as in Return of the Obra Dinn or The Roottrees Are Dead. While the game has a handful of genuinely fun puzzles and some cool twists and ideas, they're presented extremely linearly, and the latter half of this 3-hour game is basically one extended cutscene. 

Normally this wouldn't be enough for me to give a negative review, but this game explicitly markets itself as a detective game where you "solve crimes". And you really don't. For a price of about half the two aforementioned detective games, you get a fraction of the gameplay, and not that much more narrative.

Not only is the story thrilling, if predictable in its major beats, but it’s complemented by different gameplay elements with which you, as the person in the chair, become crucial to your team's success. It’s a shame you can’t spend more time with all your tech toys in extra cases that aren’t linked to the main story. I would definitely welcome a more sandboxy type of sequel or DLC, without a big conspiracy to uncover but just a bunch of standalone cases you as "The Operator" help solve. As it is, the emphasis lies on delivering a taut, intriguing cyberthriller that is highly linear but very well put together, and is sure to leave lots of gamers wanting more.

Great story, great voice acting, great gameplay but suffers from the amount of content (or lack there of).  The game gives you all sorts of fun tools, uses them once, and then the game is all but over in less than 2.5 hours, give or take.  

There are a few achievements that you can miss through the game, and the only way to get them back is to play it all over again, unskippable dialog and cut scenes from start to finish, further 'padding' the runtime.  

Ultimately, the ending is hollow and melancholic, with loose ends and threads begging to be tied up.  Overall, wasn't really worth the price of admission considering the shortness of the game.
Pretty good game, but insanely short. 3 hours, maybe 4 if you take your time.
My only complaint is that it was too short. Brilliant otherwise.
